claims.text: The material system is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The bulk specimen contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The oxygen is present as interstitial defects associated with lattice distortions.
A model incorporating explicit oxygen-defect scattering and temperature-dependent electron–phonon interactions will predict conductivity more accurately than perfect-crystal models.
The claimed accuracy improvement applies over both 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Conductivity measurements exist for approximately 1 wt.% oxygen-containing samples in both specified temperature regimes.
Impurity scattering dominates charge-carrier mobility at 0–200 K.
At 300–1200 K, phonon scattering and oxygen-induced lattice distortions both modulate the electron mean free path.
Interstitial oxygen creates additional carrier-scattering centers.
Accounting for defect and phonon effects adjusts effective carrier-scattering rates and bridges the gap between predictions and measurements.
The proposed approach will predict conductivity within approximately 10% of measured values in both temperature regimes.
Existing perfect-crystal analytical predictions exhibit substantial discrepancies from measurements when oxygen interstitials are present.
The proposed model is applicable only to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K and to specimens with oxygen content near 1 wt.%.
Predictions may be unreliable outside the stated temperature windows or at substantially different defect concentrations.
Variations in microstructure and defect clustering can change the quantitative contribution of defect scattering.
Failure to reduce conductivity-prediction discrepancy by at least 10% relative to a defect-free model in both regimes would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome uses an absolute accuracy target of within approximately 10% of measurement, whereas the falsification rule uses a relative improvement target of at least 10% over the baseline model. These are non-equivalent benchmarks and can yield conflicting pass/fail judgments.
